---
title: "Figure 5.1: Labor Productivity Gap against the United States"
---

![Python: `python/fig-5-1.py`](../images/python/fig-5-1.png)

Labor productivity in four economies, as the gap with the United States in
percent of US productivity. All gaps are negative: every region is less
productive than the United States. The three Latin American and Caribbean
groups are 50 to 75 percent below; Canada is much closer, about 25 percent
below, and is drawn on a right-hand scale so its movements remain visible.

**New in this chart:** two scales that are both entirely negative.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 8 rows (2019 to 2026):

| category | LA7 | CAPDR | CARIB | CAN (right scale) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 | -69.3 | -66.7 | -51.0 | -22.7 |

The years are numbers, so they can be used on the x-axis directly. The
column name `CAN (right scale)` comes from the Excel series name. The
extraction keeps it as it is, and the script uses it both to read the data
and as the legend label.

## The script

### The series and their colours

```python
data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

left_series = {"LA7": "#5B2A7F", "CAPDR": "#CE5A0A", "CARIB": "#009EAD"}
canada = "CAN (right scale)"
canada_colour = "#666666"
```

The three left-scale series are in one dictionary, so a loop can draw them.
Canada is kept apart, in two variables, because it is drawn on a different
axes object. Storing the long column name in `canada` once avoids typing it
again, and a typo, later.

### The frame

`new_chart()` is called with a nine-line caption, so the plot area is
shorter than usual. Two arguments are worth noting:

- `caption_size=8.4`, a little smaller than the default 8.5, so the longest
  caption line fits within the 5-inch width;
- `left=0.4` and `right=0.4`, equal margins, because both sides now carry
  tick labels such as `-75` and `-32`. The minus sign makes the labels wider
  than positive ones.

### Two scales

```python
for series, colour in left_series.items():
    ax.plot(years, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="round")

ax_right = add_right_axis(ax, (-32, -22), 2)
ax_right.plot(years, data[canada], color=canada_colour, linewidth=1.8,
              solid_capstyle="round")
ax_right.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

First the loop draws LA7, CAPDR and CARIB on `ax`, the left scale. Then
`add_right_axis()` creates `ax_right`, a second plot area on top of the
first that shares the x-axis but has its own y-axis on the right, from -32
to -22 with a tick every 2. Canada is drawn on that axes object. See [A
right-hand scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-right-axis).

The lines have no `label=` argument, because the legend is built by hand
below.

**Lining up the ticks.** The left-hand scale runs from -75 to -50 in steps
of 5 and the right-hand scale from -32 to -22 in steps of 2. Both have five
intervals, so each tick on the left is level with one on the right. This is
not automatic. If you change one scale, choose the other so that

$$\frac{\text{high} - \text{low}}{\text{step}}$$

is the same on both sides. Otherwise the ticks on the two sides fall at
different heights, which is hard to read.

**Negative scales** need no special treatment: `set_y_scale(ax, -75, -50,
5)` and `add_right_axis(ax, (-32, -22), 2)` work as for positive ones. The
lowest value is always the first argument. Because the house style turns off
`axes.unicode_minus`, the labels use a plain hyphen (`-75`) as Excel does,
not the typographic minus sign that matplotlib uses by default. See [The
house style](../chart-style.qmd#sec-rcparams).

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xlim(2018.5, 2026.5)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -75, -50, 5)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

With only eight years, every year is labelled: `ax.set_xticks(years)` puts a
tick at each value of the `category` column. The limits leave half a year of
margin at each end.

### The legend

```python
styles = {**left_series, canada: canada_colour}
ax_right.legend(
    [Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=1.8) for c in styles.values()],
    list(styles),
    loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(0.99, 0.98), handlelength=3.0,
    labelspacing=0.1,
)
```

Each axes object only knows its own lines, so neither `ax.legend()` nor
`ax_right.legend()` would list all four series. The script builds the
legend itself:

1. `{**left_series, canada: canada_colour}` makes one dictionary with all
   four names and colours, in legend order. `**` unpacks the first
   dictionary into the new one.
2. `Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=1.8)` is a line with no data, used
   only as a legend sample. The list comprehension makes one for each
   colour.
3. `list(styles)` gives the four names, in the same order.

The legend is added to `ax_right`, the axes object on top, so no line is
drawn over it. It sits in the top right, where the lines leave room. This is
the same pattern as in [Figure 3.4](fig-3-4.qmd). See [A right-hand
scale](../techniques.qmd#sec-right-scale).

## Changing the chart

- **One scale only.** If the gaps were similar in size, you would delete the
  `add_right_axis()` line, draw Canada on `ax` and give each line a `label=`.
  Then a plain `ax.legend()` is enough.
- **A different right-hand range.** Keep five intervals, for example
  `(-35, -20)` with a step of 3.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-5-1.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-5-1.py"}
"""Figure 5.1: Labor Productivity Gap against the United States."""
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from chart_style import (
    add_right_axis,
    new_chart,
    read_chart_data,
    save_chart,
    set_y_scale,
)

STEM = "fig-5-1"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

left_series = {"LA7": "#5B2A7F", "CAPDR": "#CE5A0A", "CARIB": "#009EAD"}
canada = "CAN (right scale)"
canada_colour = "#666666"

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Labor Productivity Gap against the United States",
    subtitle="(Percent of US labor productivity)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: IMF, World Economic Outlook database; and IMF staff\n"
        "calculations.\n"
        "Note: Labor productivity is measured as real GDP in PPP international\n"
        "dollars divided by total employment. The gap is measured as the\n"
        "difference in the level of labor productivity relative to the United States.\n"
        "Aggregates are purchasing-power-parity GDP-weighted averages.\n"
        "CAPDR = Central America, Panama, and the Dominican Republic; CARIB\n"
        "= Caribbean; LA7 = Latin America 7 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico,\n"
        "Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay); PPP = purchasing power parity."
    ),
    caption_size=8.4,
    left=0.4,
    right=0.4,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)

for series, colour in left_series.items():
    ax.plot(years, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.8,
            solid_capstyle="round")

ax_right = add_right_axis(ax, (-32, -22), 2)
ax_right.plot(years, data[canada], color=canada_colour, linewidth=1.8,
              solid_capstyle="round")
ax_right.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.set_xlim(2018.5, 2026.5)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -75, -50, 5)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

styles = {**left_series, canada: canada_colour}
ax_right.legend(
    [Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=1.8) for c in styles.values()],
    list(styles),
    loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(0.99, 0.98), handlelength=3.0,
    labelspacing=0.1,
)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
